topic: Change of Basis: Translating Between Mathematical Worlds
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Translating Between Mathematical Worlds
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Perspective Problem
sections.content: Introduce the concept that the same physical point can be described by different sets of coordinates depending on the 'grid' (basis) we use. Define the goal: finding the mathematical 'translator' between these grids.
sections.example: Imagine a robot named 'Z-4' standing in a room. You describe its position using the floor tiles (Standard Basis), but the robot describes positions based on its own slanted orientation (Custom Basis). The physical robot hasn't moved, but the numbers in our reports are different.

sections.title: Prerequisite: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Briefly refresh the concept of basis vectors. Visualize the standard basis (i-hat, j-hat) as a perfect square grid. Explain that any two non-parallel vectors can form a new coordinate system (a new grid).
sections.example: Visual: An animation showing the standard i=(1,0), j=(0,1) grid morphing/tilting into a new grid defined by vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1).

sections.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The Translator)
sections.content: Explain how to build the 'Transition Matrix' (P). Key Concept: The columns of this matrix are simply the new basis vectors expressed in the language of the old (standard) basis.
sections.example: If our new basis vectors are B1 = [2, 1] and B2 = [-1, 1], we line them up to create Matrix P = [[2, -1], [1, 1]]. This matrix 'translates' coordinates from the Robot's language back to our Standard language.

sections.title: The Coordinate Transformation Formula
sections.content: Introduce the formula: [x]_{standard} = P * [x]_{new}. Visualize this as taking a coordinate in the skewed grid and 'scaling/rotating' it back to the square grid.
sections.example: If the Robot says it is at position (1, 1) in its own grid, we multiply Matrix P by [1, 1]. Calculation: [2-1, 1+1] = (1, 2). Graphically show the point landing on (1, 2) on the standard XY plane.

sections.title: Reversing the Process (The Inverse)
sections.content: How do we go from Standard Basis to the New Basis? Introduce the inverse matrix (P⁻¹). Explain that if P takes us 'Home', P⁻¹ takes us 'Into the New World'.
sections.example: To tell the robot to move to our point (3, 3), we don't give it (3, 3). We multiply (3, 3) by the inverse of P to find the coordinates in the robot's specific tilted grid.

sections.title: Summary & Visual Recap
sections.content: Summarize that 'Change of Basis' is just a change of perspective. The Transition Matrix is the bridge between these perspectives. Show a final animation of a vector staying still while the background grid swaps between standard and custom.
sections.example: Analogy: It's like converting currency. The 'Value' (the vector) stays the same, but the 'Units' (the basis) change depending on which country (coordinate system) you are in.

storyboard.title: The Perspective Problem
lecture_lines: One point can have different coordinates in different grids.
We describe its position using standard floor tiles.
The robot uses its own tilted, custom grid.
animations: Show a point at (2,1) on a white square grid (#FFFFFF). Label it 'Z-4' in white (#FFFFFF).
Fade in a slanted blue grid (#5271FF) defined by basis vectors b1=(2,1) and b2=(-1,1).
Highlight coordinates (2,1) in the standard grid and (1,0) in the blue grid for the same point.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: Standard basis vectors i-hat and j-hat form squares.
Any two non-parallel vectors can form a new grid.
Let's define a new basis with two slanted vectors.
animations: Show i-hat (1,0) in green (#00FF00) and j-hat (0,1) in red (#FF0000) on a standard grid.
Morph i-hat and j-hat into b1=(2,1) in cyan (#00FFFF) and b2=(-1,1) in yellow (#FFFF00).
Expand b1 and b2 into a full skewed coordinate grid covering the screen.

storyboard.title: The Change of Basis Matrix (The Translator)
lecture_lines: Matrix P acts as a translator between these grids.
We build P using the new basis vectors.
Each new vector becomes a column in Matrix P.
These columns are written in the standard basis language.
This matrix connects the robot's world to ours.
animations: Display vectors b1=(2,1) in cyan (#00FFFF) and b2=(-1,1) in yellow (#FFFF00) as independent vectors.
Vertically align b1 and b2 to form the columns of a matrix P.
Highlight the first column (2,1) and the second column (-1,1) within the matrix P.
Label the columns of P as 'New Basis in Old Terms' using white text (#FFFFFF).
Box the entire matrix P and label it 'Transition Matrix' in white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: The Coordinate Transformation Formula
lecture_lines: We use a formula to transform between perspectives.
Multiply matrix P by the robot's coordinates.
This calculation maps the point back to standard space.
The result tells us the standard XY coordinates.
We have successfully translated the robot's location.
animations: Write the formula [x]_std = P * [x]_new at the top in white (#FFFFFF).
Show a vector x_new=(1,1) as a dot relative to the skewed grid lines.
Display the matrix multiplication [[2,-1],[1,1]] * [[1],[1]] = [[1],[2]] next to the formula.
Animate the skewed grid morphing back into the standard square grid.
Point to the final position (1,2) on the standard square grid.

storyboard.title: Reversing the Process (The Inverse)
lecture_lines: What if we want to translate into the robot's world?
We must reverse the process using the inverse matrix.
Multiply standard coordinates by the inverse of P.
This finds the coordinates in the robot's tilted grid.
Now we can communicate directions the robot understands.
animations: Display the inverse formula [x]_new = P⁻¹ * [x]_std in white (#FFFFFF).
Plot a point at (3,3) in the standard grid in orange (#FFA500).
Show the point's coordinates in the skewed grid after applying the inverse matrix P⁻¹.

storyboard.title: Summary & Visual Recap
lecture_lines: Change of basis is simply a shift in perspective.
The vector stays fixed while the grid transforms.
Think of it like converting between different currencies.
animations: Animate a fixed vector while the grid swaps between standard and skewed.
Display matrix P and P⁻¹ as arrows bridging the two coordinate systems.
Fade in the text 'Change of Perspective' in white (#FFFFFF).
